twins.questionText: A 0.2 m aqueous solution of NaCl is completely dissociated. Calculate the depression in freezing point. (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
twins.solution: NaCl gives 2 ions, so i = 2. ΔTf = iKf·m = 2 × 1.86 × 0.2 = 0.744 K.

twins.questionText: A 0.05 m aqueous solution of CaCl₂ is completely dissociated. Calculate the depression in freezing point. (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
twins.solution: CaCl₂ gives 3 ions (Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻), so i = 3. ΔTf = 3 × 1.86 × 0.05 = 0.279 K.

twins.questionText: A 0.05 m aqueous solution of AlCl₃ is completely dissociated. Calculate the depression in freezing point. (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
twins.solution: AlCl₃ gives 4 ions (Al³⁺ + 3Cl⁻), so i = 4. ΔTf = 4 × 1.86 × 0.05 = 0.372 K.

keyPoints: States Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution (p = K_H·x)
At depth, high pressure dissolves more nitrogen in the blood; on rising it forms bubbles (the bends)
Helium is much less soluble in blood, so diluting air with it reduces this risk

twins.questionText: State Henry's law. Why are soft drink bottles sealed under high pressure?
keyPoints: States Henry's law: partial pressure of a gas ∝ its mole fraction in solution (p = K_H·x)
High pressure increases the solubility of CO₂ in the drink
On opening, pressure falls, so dissolved CO₂ escapes as bubbles (fizz)
twins.solution: Henry's law: p = K_H·x. Bottles are sealed under high CO₂ pressure so more CO₂ dissolves. Opening the bottle lowers the pressure, so the gas comes out of solution as bubbles.

twins.questionText: How does temperature affect the solubility of a gas in a liquid? Why are aquatic animals more comfortable in cold water than in warm water?
keyPoints: Solubility of a gas decreases as temperature rises (K_H increases with temperature)
Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen, so more oxygen is available to aquatic animals
twins.solution: Dissolving a gas is exothermic, so solubility falls as temperature rises (K_H increases). Cold water therefore holds more dissolved O₂, which aquatic animals need.

twins.questionText: Climbers at high altitudes often feel weak and cannot think clearly (anoxia). Explain using Henry's law.
keyPoints: At high altitude the partial pressure of oxygen is lower
By Henry's law less oxygen dissolves in the blood
Low oxygen in the blood and tissues causes weakness and poor thinking (anoxia)
twins.solution: Partial pressure of O₂ is low at high altitude. By Henry's law, the amount of O₂ dissolved in blood is proportional to that partial pressure, so blood carries less oxygen, causing anoxia.

twins.questionText: 1.0 g of a polymer dissolved in 500 mL of solution has an osmotic pressure of 0.00166 bar at 300 K. Calculate its molar mass. (R = 0.083 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
0.5 g of a protein in 100 mL of solution has an osmotic pressure of 0.00249 bar at 27 °C. Calculate its molar mass. (R = 0.083 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
2.5 g of a polymer in 200 mL of solution has an osmotic pressure of 0.0083 bar at 300 K. Calculate its molar mass. (R = 0.083 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
Calculate the standard cell potential for Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu. (E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.37 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V)
twins.solution: Mg is oxidised (anode), Cu²⁺ is reduced (cathode). E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−2.37) = +2.71 V.

twins.questionText: Calculate the standard cell potential for Fe + 2Ag⁺ → Fe²⁺ + 2Ag. (E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V, E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V)
twins.solution: Fe is the anode, Ag the cathode. E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.44) = +1.24 V. E° is not doubled for 2Ag⁺.

twins.questionText: Calculate E°cell for the cell Ni(s)|Ni²⁺(aq)||Cu²⁺(aq)|Cu(s). (E°(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.25 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V)
twins.solution: The left electrode is the anode. E°cell = E°right − E°left = 0.34 − (−0.25) = +0.59 V.

twins.questionText: Calculate the emf at 298 K of Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(0.01 M)||Ag⁺(0.1 M)|Ag(s). (E°cell = 1.56 V)
twins.solution: Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag, n = 2. Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Ag⁺]² = 0.01/(0.1)² = 1, so log Q = 0 and E = 1.56 V.

twins.questionText: Calculate the emf at 298 K of Mg(s)|Mg²⁺(0.001 M)||Cu²⁺(0.0001 M)|Cu(s). (E°cell = 2.71 V)
Calculate the emf at 298 K of Cu(s)|Cu²⁺(0.01 M)||Ag⁺(0.001 M)|Ag(s). (E°cell = 0.46 V)
The conductivity of 0.05 M NaCl solution is 0.0055 S cm⁻¹. Calculate its molar conductivity.
twins.solution: Λm = κ × 1000/C = 0.0055 × 1000/0.05 = 110 S cm² mol⁻¹. The 1000 converts mol L⁻¹ to mol cm⁻³.

twins.questionText: The conductivity of 0.001 M KCl solution is 1.47 × 10⁻⁴ S cm⁻¹. Calculate its molar conductivity.
A 0.1 M solution of an electrolyte has a conductivity of 0.0106 S cm⁻¹. Calculate its molar conductivity.
For Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu, E°cell = 2.71 V. Calculate ΔrG°. (F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
twins.solution: Two electrons are transferred, n = 2. ΔrG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96500 × 2.71 = −523030 J mol⁻¹ ≈ −523.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

twins.questionText: For Fe + 2Ag⁺ → Fe²⁺ + 2Ag, E°cell = 1.24 V. Calculate ΔrG°. (F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
twins.solution: Fe → Fe²⁺ releases 2 electrons, so n = 2. ΔrG° = −2 × 96500 × 1.24 = −239320 J mol⁻¹ ≈ −239.3 kJ mol⁻¹.

twins.questionText: For 2Al + 3Cu²⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3Cu, E°cell = 2.00 V. Calculate ΔrG°. (F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
twins.solution: 2 Al atoms each lose 3 electrons, so n = 6. ΔrG° = −6 × 96500 × 2.00 = −1158000 J mol⁻¹ = −1158 kJ mol⁻¹.

twins.questionText: A first order reaction has k = 6.93 × 10⁻³ min⁻¹. Calculate its half-life.
twins.solution: For first order, t½ = 0.693/k = 0.693/(6.93 × 10⁻³) = 100 min.

twins.questionText: A first order reaction has k = 1.386 × 10⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate its half-life.
The rate constant of a first order decomposition is 0.0231 h⁻¹. Calculate its half-life.
twins.solution: t½ = 0.693/0.0231 = 30 h. (2.303 appears in the integrated rate law, not in t½ = 0.693/k.)

keyPoints: Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3
Units of k = (mol L⁻¹)¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹ = L² mol⁻² s⁻¹

twins.questionText: For rate = k[A]^½[B], give the overall order and the units of k.
keyPoints: Overall order = ½ + 1 = 3/2
Units of k = mol^(−½) L^(½) s⁻¹
twins.solution: Order = 3/2. Units: (mol L⁻¹)^(1 − 3/2) s⁻¹ = (mol L⁻¹)^(−½) s⁻¹ = mol^(−½) L^(½) s⁻¹.

twins.questionText: For a zero order reaction, rate = k. Give the units of k.
keyPoints: Overall order = 0
Units of k = mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (same as the rate)
twins.solution: For n = 0, units = (mol L⁻¹)^(1 − 0) s⁻¹ = mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

twins.questionText: For rate = k[A][B], give the overall order and the units of k.
keyPoints: Overall order = 1 + 1 = 2
Units of k = L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
twins.solution: Order = 2. Units = (mol L⁻¹)^(1 − 2) s⁻¹ = L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

twins.questionText: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Fe²⁺. (Z of Fe = 26)
twins.solution: Fe is 3d⁶4s². Fe²⁺ loses the two 4s electrons first: 3d⁶, 4 unpaired. μ = √(4 × 6) = √24 = 4.90 BM.

twins.questionText: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Cr³⁺. (Z of Cr = 24)
twins.solution: Cr is 3d⁵4s¹. Cr³⁺ loses 4s¹ and two 3d electrons: 3d³, 3 unpaired. μ = √15 = 3.87 BM.

twins.questionText: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Cu²⁺. (Z of Cu = 29)
twins.solution: Cu is 3d¹⁰4s¹. Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ with 1 unpaired electron. μ = √3 = 1.73 BM.

keyPoints: Cr²⁺ → Cr³⁺ gives d³, a stable half-filled t₂g level, so Cr²⁺ readily loses an electron (reducing)
Mn³⁺ → Mn²⁺ gives d⁵, a stable half-filled configuration, so Mn³⁺ readily gains an electron (oxidising)

twins.questionText: Why is Mn²⁺ much more resistant to oxidation than Fe²⁺?
keyPoints: Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵, an extra-stable half-filled configuration, so removing an electron is hard
Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶; losing one electron gives Fe³⁺ (3d⁵), which is stable, so Fe²⁺ is easily oxidised
twins.solution: Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) is already half-filled and stable. Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) becomes the stable half-filled 3d⁵ on oxidation, so it oxidises easily.

twins.questionText: E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) = +1.57 V is much more positive than E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V. Explain.
keyPoints: Mn³⁺ → Mn²⁺ produces the stable half-filled d⁵ configuration, so Mn³⁺ is very easily reduced (large positive E°)
Fe³⁺ is already d⁵; reducing it to Fe²⁺ (d⁶) loses that stability, so the value is smaller
twins.solution: Reduction of Mn³⁺ (d⁴) gives stable Mn²⁺ (d⁵), so it is strongly favoured. Reduction of Fe³⁺ (d⁵) destroys a half-filled shell, so it is less favoured.

twins.questionText: Why is E°(Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺) negative (−0.41 V)?
keyPoints: Cr³⁺ has the stable half-filled t₂g³ configuration, so it is not easily reduced
Cr²⁺ readily loses an electron to reach this stable state, so the couple has a negative E°
twins.solution: Cr³⁺ (t₂g³) is stable, so Cr³⁺ resists reduction and Cr²⁺ is a good reducing agent. Hence E°(Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺) is negative.

keyPoints: Ligand named 'cyanido' with the prefix hexa-
Anionic complex named 'ferrate' with oxidation state (III): potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)

twins.questionText: Write the IUPAC name of K₄[Fe(CN)₆].
keyPoints: Ligand named 'hexacyanido'
Anionic complex 'ferrate' with oxidation state (II): potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)
twins.solution: Fe is +2 (4 × 1 + x + 6 × (−1) = 0). Name: potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II).

twins.questionText: Write the IUPAC name of [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃.
keyPoints: Ligand named 'hexaammine'
Cationic complex keeps the metal name 'cobalt' with (III): hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride
twins.solution: The complex ion is a cation, so the metal keeps its name. Co is +3. Name: hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride.

twins.questionText: Write the IUPAC name of K₂[PtCl₆].
keyPoints: Ligand named 'hexachlorido'
Anionic complex 'platinate' with oxidation state (IV): potassium hexachloridoplatinate(IV)
twins.solution: Pt is +4 (2 + x − 6 = 0). The complex is an anion, so -ate is used. Name: potassium hexachloridoplatinate(IV).

keyPoints: In [Ni(CO)₄], Ni is 0; strong-field CO pairs the electrons (3d¹⁰), sp³, no unpaired electrons, so it is diamagnetic
In [NiCl₄]²⁻, Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸; weak-field Cl⁻ cannot force pairing, leaving 2 unpaired electrons (sp³), so it is paramagnetic

twins.questionText: [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ is weakly paramagnetic while [FeF₆]³⁻ is strongly paramagnetic. Explain.
keyPoints: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ in both complexes
Strong-field CN⁻ forces pairing: inner orbital d²sp³, 1 unpaired electron (weakly paramagnetic)
Weak-field F⁻ does not: outer orbital sp³d², 5 unpaired electrons (strongly paramagnetic)
twins.solution: Fe³⁺ (3d⁵). With CN⁻, electrons pair in t₂g (t₂g⁵), d²sp³, one unpaired electron. With F⁻ there is no pairing, sp³d², five unpaired electrons.

twins.questionText: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is diamagnetic but [CoF₆]³⁻ is paramagnetic. Explain.
keyPoints: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶ in both
NH₃ is strong field here: all six electrons pair (t₂g⁶), d²sp³, no unpaired electrons, so diamagnetic
F⁻ is weak field: 4 unpaired electrons, sp³d², so paramagnetic
twins.solution: Co³⁺ (3d⁶). NH₃ causes pairing: t₂g⁶eg⁰, inner orbital d²sp³, diamagnetic. F⁻ does not: t₂g⁴eg², four unpaired electrons, outer orbital sp³d².

twins.questionText: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is diamagnetic and square planar, while [NiCl₄]²⁻ is paramagnetic and tetrahedral. Explain.
keyPoints: Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸ in both
Strong-field CN⁻ pairs the electrons, freeing one 3d orbital: dsp², square planar, no unpaired electrons
Weak-field Cl⁻ cannot pair them: 2 unpaired electrons, sp³, tetrahedral
twins.solution: Ni²⁺ (3d⁸). CN⁻ pairs the two unpaired electrons, so one 3d orbital joins dsp² hybridisation (square planar, diamagnetic). Cl⁻ cannot, so sp³ (tetrahedral) with two unpaired electrons.

keyPoints: Correct order: (CH₃)₃CBr < (CH₃)₂CHBr < CH₃CH₂Br < CH₃Br
Reason: SN2 needs backside attack, so steric hindrance (not carbocation stability) decides the order

twins.questionText: Arrange 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in increasing order of SN2 reactivity.
keyPoints: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane < 2-bromobutane < 1-bromobutane
Reason: more alkyl groups around the reacting carbon block backside attack (steric hindrance)
twins.solution: 3° < 2° < 1° for SN2, because bulky groups hinder the nucleophile approaching from the back.

twins.questionText: Arrange 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in increasing order of SN1 reactivity.
keyPoints: 1-bromobutane < 2-bromobutane < 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
Reason: SN1 goes through a carbocation, and a 3° carbocation is the most stable
twins.solution: For SN1 the order reverses: 1° < 2° < 3°, because the rate depends on carbocation stability. Compare with SN2, where steric hindrance decides.

twins.questionText: Which reacts faster by SN2 with OH⁻: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br or (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br? Give the reason.
keyPoints: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br reacts faster
Both are primary, but branching next to the reacting carbon in (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br increases steric hindrance to backside attack
twins.solution: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br. Both are 1° halides, but the branched one has a bulky isopropyl group next to the C–Br carbon, which hinders the nucleophile.

keyPoints: Both have the same molar mass (C₂H₆O), so mass is not the reason
Ethanol forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds through its –OH group; methoxymethane cannot hydrogen bond with itself

twins.questionText: Propan-1-ol (M = 60) boils at 370 K but butane (M = 58) boils at 273 K. Explain.
keyPoints: Their molar masses are almost the same, so mass does not explain the difference
Propan-1-ol molecules are held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds through –OH; butane has only weak van der Waals forces
twins.solution: Similar masses, very different forces: hydrogen bonding in propan-1-ol needs much more energy to break than the dispersion forces in butane.

twins.questionText: Arrange butane, methoxyethane and propan-1-ol in increasing order of boiling point, with a reason.
keyPoints: Butane < methoxyethane < propan-1-ol
Methoxyethane is polar (dipole–dipole) but cannot H-bond with itself; propan-1-ol forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds
twins.solution: All have M ≈ 58–60. Butane: dispersion only. Methoxyethane: dipole–dipole. Propan-1-ol: hydrogen bonding, so it boils highest.

twins.questionText: o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile but p-nitrophenol is not. Explain.
keyPoints: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, so its molecules do not associate
p-Nitrophenol forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds, so molecules associate and it is less volatile
twins.solution: In the ortho isomer the –OH bonds to the neighbouring –NO₂ inside the same molecule. In the para isomer they are too far apart, so molecules bond to each other.

keyPoints: Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction (not aldol)
Products: benzyl alcohol (C₆H₅CH₂OH) and sodium benzoate (C₆H₅COONa)

twins.questionText: Write the products when formaldehyde (HCHO) is treated with concentrated NaOH.
keyPoints: No α-hydrogen, so Cannizzaro reaction
Products: methanol (CH₃OH) and sodium formate (HCOONa)
twins.solution: 2HCHO + conc. NaOH → CH₃OH + HCOONa. One molecule is reduced, the other oxidised.

twins.questionText: Which of ethanal, methanal and benzaldehyde undergo aldol condensation and which undergo the Cannizzaro reaction? Give a reason.
keyPoints: Ethanal has α-hydrogens, so it undergoes aldol condensation
Methanal and benzaldehyde have no α-hydrogen, so they undergo the Cannizzaro reaction
twins.solution: Aldol needs an α-hydrogen to form an enolate. Without one, concentrated alkali causes the Cannizzaro reaction instead.

twins.questionText: What happens when ethanal is treated with dilute NaOH?
keyPoints: Ethanal has α-hydrogens, so aldol condensation occurs
Product is 3-hydroxybutanal (aldol), which on heating gives but-2-enal
twins.solution: 2CH₃CHO → (dil. NaOH) CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO (3-hydroxybutanal) → (heat, −H₂O) CH₃CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal).

keyPoints: The carbonyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing
The conjugate base (enolate ion) is stabilised by resonance

twins.questionText: Why are the α-hydrogens of propanone acidic, while the hydrogens of propane are not?
keyPoints: The C=O group withdraws electrons from the α-carbon
The enolate ion formed is resonance stabilised; propane has no such group or stabilisation
twins.solution: In propanone the carbonyl pulls electron density and the resulting enolate spreads its charge onto oxygen by resonance. Propane has neither feature.

twins.questionText: Why are carboxylic acids more acidic than alcohols?
keyPoints: The carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance: the negative charge is shared equally by two oxygen atoms
The alkoxide ion has no resonance stabilisation (and alkyl groups push electrons onto it)
twins.solution: RCOO⁻ has two equivalent resonance structures, so it is a stable conjugate base. RO⁻ has its charge on one oxygen only.

twins.questionText: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
keyPoints: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance (charge delocalised into the ring)
The ethoxide ion has no resonance, and the ethyl group is electron-donating, which destabilises it
twins.solution: A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid. Phenoxide is resonance stabilised; ethoxide is not.

keyPoints: Aniline is a Lewis base and reacts with the Lewis acid catalyst AlCl₃ to form a salt
The nitrogen then becomes positive, which strongly deactivates the ring, so the reaction fails

twins.questionText: Why does direct nitration of aniline give a large amount of m-nitroaniline, though –NH₂ is o/p-directing?
keyPoints: In the strongly acidic nitrating mixture, aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion (–NH₃⁺)
–NH₃⁺ is deactivating and meta-directing, so a lot of meta product forms
twins.solution: Basic –NH₂ takes a proton from the acid. The anilinium ion directs to the meta position, giving about 47% m-nitroaniline.

twins.questionText: Why is the –NH₂ group of aniline acetylated before nitration?
keyPoints: Acetylation lowers the activating effect and stops –NH₂ reacting with the acid (protonation) or being oxidised
The acetanilide then gives mainly the p-nitro product, which is hydrolysed back to p-nitroaniline
twins.solution: The lone pair of N in acetanilide is shared with the C=O group, so it is less basic and less activating. Nitration becomes controlled and mainly para.

twins.questionText: Why does aniline dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid?
keyPoints: The –NH₂ nitrogen has a lone pair, so aniline is a base
It accepts H⁺ to form anilinium chloride, a water-soluble salt
twins.solution: C₆H₅NH₂ + HCl → C₆H₅NH₃⁺Cl⁻. The ionic salt dissolves in water.

keyPoints: Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises only the –CHO group to –COOH
Product is gluconic acid, HOCH₂(CHOH)₄COOH

twins.questionText: What happens when glucose is oxidised with nitric acid?
keyPoints: Nitric acid is a strong oxidant: it oxidises both the –CHO and the terminal –CH₂OH to –COOH
Product is saccharic (glucaric) acid, HOOC(CHOH)₄COOH
twins.solution: Compare with bromine water, which only oxidises –CHO (gluconic acid). HNO₃ oxidises both ends.

twins.questionText: What does the reaction of glucose with bromine water tell us about its structure?
keyPoints: A mild oxidant converts glucose to gluconic acid without losing carbon
So the carbonyl group in glucose is an aldehyde (–CHO) group
twins.solution: Only aldehydes are oxidised by bromine water. Getting gluconic acid with the same six carbons shows glucose has a –CHO group.

twins.questionText: What happens when glucose is treated with Tollens’ reagent?
keyPoints: The –CHO group is oxidised to –COOH (gluconic acid / gluconate)
Ag⁺ is reduced to metallic silver, giving a silver mirror
twins.solution: Glucose is a reducing sugar because of its aldehyde group. It reduces Tollens’ reagent to a silver mirror and is itself oxidised to gluconic acid.

keyPoints: Correct conclusion: R is not transitive
Gives a valid counterexample, e.g. (3, −2) ∈ R and (−2, 1) ∈ R but (3, 1) ∉ R

twins.questionText: Check whether R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b³} on R is transitive.
keyPoints: Correct conclusion: not transitive
Valid counterexample, e.g. (3, 3/2) ∈ R and (3/2, 6/5) ∈ R but (3, 6/5) ∉ R

twins.questionText: Check whether R = {(a, b) : b = a + 1} on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} is transitive.
keyPoints: Correct conclusion: not transitive
Valid counterexample, e.g. (1, 2) ∈ R and (2, 3) ∈ R but (1, 3) ∉ R

twins.questionText: Check whether R = {(a, b) : a − b is divisible by 3} on Z is transitive.
keyPoints: Correct conclusion: transitive
Proof: a − b = 3k and b − c = 3m give a − c = 3(k + m), so (a, c) ∈ R
twins.solution: Adding the two conditions: a − c = (a − b) + (b − c) = 3(k + m), divisible by 3. A general proof is needed; examples alone do not prove transitivity.

keyPoints: One-one: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ 4x₁ + 3 = 4x₂ + 3 ⇒ x₁ = x₂
Onto: for any y ∈ R, x = (y − 3)/4 ∈ R and f(x) = y
Conclusion: f is one-one and onto (bijective)

twins.questionText: Show that f: R → R, f(x) = 3 − 4x is one-one and onto.
keyPoints: One-one: 3 − 4x₁ = 3 − 4x₂ ⇒ x₁ = x₂
Onto: for any y ∈ R, x = (3 − y)/4 ∈ R and f(x) = y
Conclusion: f is bijective
twins.solution: One-one from cancelling. Onto by solving y = 3 − 4x for x and checking x is real. Both parts must be shown.

twins.questionText: Show that f: R → R, f(x) = 2x − 7 is a bijection.
keyPoints: One-one: 2x₁ − 7 = 2x₂ − 7 ⇒ x₁ = x₂
Onto: for any y ∈ R, x = (y + 7)/2 ∈ R and f(x) = y
Conclusion: f is bijective
twins.solution: Show one-one and onto separately. A graph or "it is a straight line" is not a proof.

twins.questionText: Is f: N → N, f(x) = 2x one-one? Is it onto? Justify.
keyPoints: One-one: 2x₁ = 2x₂ ⇒ x₁ = x₂
Not onto: e.g. y = 3 has no x ∈ N with 2x = 3 (odd numbers have no pre-image)
twins.solution: One-one but not onto. The onto step must check that x lies in the domain N, and x = 3/2 does not.

twins.questionText: If A = [1 2; 3 4] (rows separated by ;), find A².
twins.solution: A² = A·A = [1·1 + 2·3, 1·2 + 2·4; 3·1 + 4·3, 3·2 + 4·4] = [7 10; 15 22]. Multiply rows by columns; never square each entry.

twins.questionText: If A = [3 −1; 2 0] (rows separated by ;), find A².
If A = [0 1; 1 1] (rows separated by ;), find A².

keyPoints: (AB)′ = B′A′: the transpose of a product reverses the order

twins.questionText: Write (ABC)′ in terms of A′, B′ and C′.
keyPoints: (ABC)′ = C′B′A′ (the order reverses)

twins.questionText: If A is a symmetric matrix, show that B′AB is symmetric (B is a square matrix of the same order).
keyPoints: Uses the reversal rule: (B′AB)′ = B′A′(B′)′
Uses A′ = A and (B′)′ = B to get (B′AB)′ = B′AB
twins.solution: (B′AB)′ = B′A′(B′)′ = B′AB, since A′ = A. So B′AB is symmetric.

twins.questionText: A is of order 3 × 2 and B is of order 2 × 3. Is (AB)′ = A′B′ defined and equal? Write the correct expression.
keyPoints: A′B′ is (2 × 3)(3 × 2) = 2 × 2, but (AB)′ is 3 × 3, so they cannot be equal
Correct: (AB)′ = B′A′, which is (3 × 2)(2 × 3) = 3 × 3
twins.solution: AB is 3 × 3, so (AB)′ is 3 × 3. B′A′ is also 3 × 3 and equals (AB)′. A′B′ has the wrong order.

twins.questionText: A is a square matrix of order 2 with |A| = 4. Find |5A|.
twins.solution: |kA| = kⁿ|A| for order n. Here n = 2: |5A| = 5² × 4 = 100.

twins.questionText: A is a square matrix of order 3 with |A| = −2. Find |2A|.
A is a square matrix of order 3 with |A| = 3. Find |−A|.
twins.solution: |−A| = (−1)³|A| = −3. For odd order the sign changes.

Find the cofactor of a₂₃ in [2 1 3; 4 −1 0; 5 3 1] (rows separated by ;).

keyPoints: Total flux through the closed cube is q/ε₀ (Gauss's law)
By symmetry the 6 faces share it equally, so one face gets q/(6ε₀)

twins.questionText: A point charge at the centre of a cube gives a total flux of 1.2 × 10³ N m² C⁻¹ through the cube. Find the flux through one face.

parts.label: Flux through one face (N m² C⁻¹)

twins.solution: The six faces are identical and symmetric about the charge, so each gets 1.2 × 10³ / 6 = 200 N m² C⁻¹.

twins.questionText: A charge q is placed at one corner of a cube. Find the electric flux through the whole cube.
keyPoints: Imagine 8 identical cubes around the corner, which together enclose q symmetrically (total flux q/ε₀)
So this one cube gets q/(8ε₀)
twins.solution: Eight cubes meet at a corner. By symmetry each receives one eighth of q/ε₀, i.e. q/(8ε₀).

twins.questionText: A charge q is at the centre of a sphere of radius R. How does the flux through the sphere change if R is doubled?
keyPoints: No change
Flux depends only on the enclosed charge: Φ = q/ε₀ (Gauss's law), not on the size of the surface
twins.solution: The enclosed charge is unchanged, so the flux stays q/ε₀.

twins.questionText: Find the force between charges of 4 μC and 5 μC placed 20 cm apart in air.
Find the force between charges of 1 μC and 8 μC placed 40 cm apart in air.
Find the force between charges of 3 nC and 6 nC placed 3 cm apart in air.
A 4 μF capacitor is charged to 200 V and the battery is removed. A dielectric of K = 2 then fills the gap. Find the new stored energy.
twins.solution: U₀ = ½CV² = 0.08 J. Battery removed, so Q is fixed and C becomes KC: U = Q²/(2KC) = U₀/K = 0.04 J.

twins.questionText: A 2 μF capacitor is connected to a 100 V battery, which stays connected while a dielectric of K = 4 fills the gap. Find the new stored energy.
twins.solution: Battery connected, so V is fixed. C becomes KC: U = ½KCV² = K × U₀ = 4 × 0.01 = 0.04 J.

twins.questionText: A 10 μF capacitor is charged to 50 V and isolated. A dielectric of K = 5 is then inserted. Find the new stored energy.
twins.solution: U₀ = ½ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 0.0125 J. Isolated means Q is fixed, so U = U₀/K = 0.0025 J.

twins.questionText: Charges of +3 nC and −1 nC are 20 cm apart. Find the electric potential at the midpoint.
twins.solution: Potential is a scalar with sign. r = 0.1 m. V = 9 × 10⁹ × (3 − 1) × 10⁻⁹ / 0.1 = 180 V.

twins.questionText: Charges of +2 nC and +2 nC are 10 cm apart. Find the electric potential at the midpoint.
twins.solution: Both are positive, so the potentials add: 360 + 360 = 720 V.

A wire of resistance 12 Ω is cut into 3 equal parts and the parts are joined in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
twins.solution: Each part is 12/3 = 4 Ω. Three equal 4 Ω resistors in parallel: 4/3 ≈ 1.33 Ω.

twins.questionText: A wire of resistance 18 Ω is cut into 2 equal parts and the parts are joined in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
twins.solution: Each part is 9 Ω. Two in parallel: 9/2 = 4.5 Ω.

twins.questionText: A wire of resistance 20 Ω is cut into 5 equal parts and the parts are joined in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
twins.solution: Each part is 4 Ω. Five in parallel: 4/5 = 0.8 Ω. Cutting into n parts and joining in parallel gives R/n².

twins.questionText: A 6 V battery of internal resistance 0.5 Ω is being charged with a current of 2 A. Find its terminal voltage.
twins.solution: While charging, current is pushed in against the emf: V = ε + Ir = 6 + 2 × 0.5 = 7 V.

twins.questionText: A 9 V battery of internal resistance 1 Ω supplies 0.5 A to an external circuit. Find its terminal voltage.
twins.solution: While discharging, V = ε − Ir = 9 − 0.5 = 8.5 V. Compare with charging, where Ir is added.

twins.questionText: A 24 V battery of internal resistance 0.4 Ω is being charged with a current of 5 A. Find its terminal voltage.
twins.solution: Charging: V = ε + Ir = 24 + 5 × 0.4 = 26 V.

keyPoints: E = V/l, so doubling l at constant V halves the electric field
v_d = eEτ/m ∝ E, so the drift speed becomes half

twins.questionText: The potential difference across a conductor is doubled, keeping everything else the same. How does the drift speed change?
keyPoints: E = V/l doubles
v_d = eEτ/m ∝ E, so the drift speed doubles
twins.solution: Doubling V doubles E, and drift speed is proportional to E.

twins.questionText: The cross-sectional area of a wire is doubled while the potential difference across it is kept constant. How does the drift speed change?
keyPoints: E = V/l does not depend on the area, so E is unchanged
So v_d = eEτ/m is unchanged (the current doubles instead)
twins.solution: v_d depends on E, which depends on V and l only. A larger area carries more current at the same drift speed.

twins.questionText: The temperature of a metal wire rises while the potential difference across it is kept constant. How does the drift speed change?
keyPoints: Electrons collide more often, so the relaxation time τ decreases
v_d = eEτ/m, so the drift speed decreases
twins.solution: E is unchanged, but τ falls with temperature, so v_d falls (resistance rises).

twins.questionText: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image distance v (with sign).
twins.solution: u = −30 cm, f = −20 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/30 = −1/60, so v = −60 cm: real, inverted, in front of the mirror.

twins.questionText: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the image distance v (with sign).
twins.solution: u = −20 cm, f = +15 cm (convex). 1/v = 1/15 + 1/20 = 7/60, so v = +8.57 cm: virtual, erect, behind the mirror.

twins.questionText: An object is placed 5 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance v (with sign).
twins.solution: u = −5 cm, f = −10 cm. 1/v = −1/10 + 1/5 = 1/10, so v = +10 cm: virtual, erect, behind the mirror (object inside f).
